title: Body
hookLine: the body as a temple: sleep, food, movement
tomorrow: Jesus gives thanks for five loaves. why thank God for so little?

lines: NO SLEEP, WORN LIKE A BADGE.
cards: Running on almost no sleep gets worn like a badge sometimes. The prophet Elijah hits the bottom of that.
Worn out and running for his life, he sits under a juniper tree in the wilderness and asks to die: “It is enough; now, O LORD, take away my life.” What comes next is not a lecture. He falls asleep.
An angel touches him and says, “Arise and eat.” Bread, water, more sleep, more food. Only then, the journey.

teach.h: A TEMPLE OF THE HOLY GHOST.
teach.b: So, one question: is caring for the body holy, or just maintenance?

Paul answers it in a letter to Corinth: “What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own?” A temple: a place where God is honored.
Sleep, food and movement become ways of keeping that place.
A psalm says it with wonder: “I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.” Now a neighbor who says something close.
In an old Jewish midrash, the sage Hillel is walking with his students and tells them he's off to do a mitzvah, a commanded good deed. Which one? Bathing.
If the keepers of a king's statues wash them, how much more a person, since the Torah says, in the old Jewish translation, “for in the image of God made He man.”
Shared: caring for the body is not vanity; it's honoring what God made. One honest difference.
Hillel's reason is the image of God, which Christians read in Genesis too.
Paul adds a Christian claim, the Holy Spirit dwelling within, a body “bought with a price.” And if Elijah's low place is ever yours, reach out: call or text 988 in the US, or local emergency help.

how: Christians care for the body in different ways: grace before meals, Sunday rest, fasting in some seasons and feasting in others; some churches anoint the sick with oil and pray for healing.

o: a temple to keep: slept, fed and moved with care
a project to perfect so others admire it
a shell the soul is waiting to leave behind

games.q: keeping the temple — tap the pairs.

s: caring for your body is vanity, not faith
Paul calls the body a temple, and in the midrash Hillel calls bathing a good deed.
in 1 Kings, the angel's first gifts to Elijah are sleep and food
he slept under a juniper tree; an angel touched him and said, arise and eat.
Hillel's reason for washing is that people are made in God's image
his verse: for in the image of God made He man.

games.q: a Jewish classmate skips a late party to sleep before a big test, and says looking after his body is a mitzvah. a friend rolls her eyes. what would Hillel's story tell her?
o: in his tradition, caring for a body made in God's image is a good deed.
he's using religion as an excuse to leave early and study.
that idea only comes from the Christian picture of a temple.
games.why: in the midrash Hillel calls bathing a mitzvah, because people are made in the image of God. Christians share that image, and Paul adds the temple.

practice: Close your eyes and travel slowly through your body, from your feet up to your forehead. Notice where it's tired, without fixing anything yet. Before you open your eyes, choose tonight's bedtime, a little earlier than usual.

wordCard.voice: Body. Not a shell to drag around, but a temple to keep: slept, fed and moved with care.

orig.note: Greek: temple, the inner sanctuary. Paul's word for the body in 1 Corinthians 6:19.

carryVoice: Keep this one: care for the temple, starting with an earlier bedtime tonight. Day 1728, kept.
